entry.title: Magnetic-field-induced nonlocal transport in the topological semimetal ZrTe5

link.title: Magnetic-field-induced nonlocal transport in the topological semimetal ZrTe5

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 24

Today’s paper was very interesting to me, because it is the closest thing I could find to someone already having performed the experiments I am (likely) going to do during my PhD programme. The material’s not the same (at least I don’t think so, I don’t actually know yet), but it is a topological semimetal, so that’s probably the best I’m gonna find in the literature.

In short, the authors took some pieces of ZrTe5 crystal and placed up to 8 electrodes on them parallel to each other. They passed current between electrodes 1 and 2, and then detected nonzero voltages between electrode 8 and all the others, exponentially decaying with distance from the current drain (electrode 2). The nonlocal voltage was detected only when there was an external magnetic field parallel to the a axis of the crystal, if the field direction was more than 1° off, the effect vanished. They also did some more standard Hall bar measurements, and also got a nonzero voltage across the bar away from the charge current. According to their simulations, the trivial explanations – inhomogeneous current distribution and hence just Ohm’s law, and Joule heating of the bar creating temperature gradients – produce a decay length that is way smaller than the one they observed. Spin diffusion length in this material is known to be much larger than the ones they measured. So they conjectured the observed effects were a result of the current in zirconium pentatelluride polarizing some other degree of freedom (not spin) and this polarization travelling along the sample, in an effect similar to SHE. I’m not sure what to think about the results, really, I’m out of my depth here. But the experiment design feels to me like something worth stealing.

entry.title: Spin Hall effect
entry.content:
A paper a day: day 23

Today’s paper took me more than a week to read, and to be completely honest, I still have not finished certain parts, mainly in the theory section. It is a survey of the whole spin Hall effect field circa ten years ago, written by people who played a big role in creating it. As such, it is both way too big to grasp quickly and way too small to cover everything in any sort of detail. It was very painful to read at times: I’d very much rather read several papers, each covering its own tiny topic, than one that jumps all over the place. Despite that, I am positive I will return to this one many dozens of times, because it is kind of a “table of contents” for the whole field. I’ll open it just for the bibliography, if nothing else.

entry.title: Spin-polarized electron transport for the altermagnet CrSb

link.title: Spin-polarized electron transport for the altermagnet CrSb

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 21

Today’s paper is yet another work-related one, but now in a slightly different way: it was written by my advisor’s group. It is related to what I’ll be doing, though, so it was doubly useful (to be fair, my advisor was the one who sent it to me, so that was a gimme).

The object under study – chromium antimonide – is altermagnetic. That means, among other things, that it does not have a net magnetic moment (like antiferromagnets), but the spin degeneracy is broken in most of the Brillouin zone (except for momenta that are time-reversal invariant by themselves). The absense of net magnetisation means there shouldn’t be much anomalous Hall effect to speak of. And indeed there isn’t: when a CrSb flake was placed on gold leads, and AC current passed through it, there was no measurable transverse voltage. However, when nickel leads were used instead, and the whole assembly placed inside a magnetic field, there was a measurable, albeit very noisy, AHE signal. Why? Because Ni is ferromagnetic, and the current passed through it is thus spin-polarised.

Nonlinear Hall effect arises from broken inversion symmetry just as anomalous Hall effect arises from broken time-reversal symmetry. I am not quite up to speed on the theory of all this (and seems likely some of the future papers here will come from me struggling to understand it), but from what I gathered so far, the equation for electron’s velocity in a crystal has a term \(\dot{\textbf{k}} \times \textbf{\Omega}_k\), and a bunch of mathemagic later you get that if inversion symmetry is broken, there is a transverse current at twice the frequency. CrSb is inversion symmetric, so there should not be much second harmonic transverse voltage if the sample is placed onto gold leads. There is some, for reasons unclear to me, and not really explained in the paper (I’ve seen other papers that claim detection of NLHE in inversion symmetric materials, but I haven’t yet read any), but regardless, with ferromagnetic leads the measured second harmonic response is much more pronounced.

The thing I find sorely lacking in this paper is a quantitative description of what the various curves they measured are expected to look like. So far it is only qualitative. I guess, if I’m gonna be doing related work, I’ll find a friendly theoretical physicist that would explain (or produce?) models for this sort of stuff for me.

entry.title: Collatz, but stop at the drop

link.title: Collatz, but stop at the drop

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 22

Today’s paper comes to me from Sequence Fanatics mailing list, of which I’ve been a member (mostly lurking) for almost six years now. It’s a place of informal conversation for contributors of OEIS – Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, and one of my favourite places to browse for interesting maths. This paper is “aimed to be enjoyed by teenagers and other playful people” and sure enough I enjoyed it a lot. I never was particularly interested in Collatz, but this paper managed to cast the problem in a different light. Just rephrase it as “every number above one eventually drops to a smaller number” and suddenly there appears a very approachable universe. Still rich and vast and not fully explored, this is Collatz we’re talking ‘bout after all, but approachable!

entry.title: Spin Hall effect, Hall effect and spin precession in diffusive normal metals

link.title: Spin Hall effect, Hall effect and spin precession in diffusive normal metals

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 20

Today’s paper I read trying to find where the value for spin-orbit coupling constant in aluminum \(\alpha=0.006\) comes from (question arose while reading another paper, where there was an aluminum Hall cross, and there was a tiny but measurable spin Hall transverse voltage). That question is stil unanswered, I’ve still no clue who’s measurements produced that value, but this paper explained a bit of theory I had troubles with. As, for instance the precise nature of the dimensionless coupling constant \(\alpha\) itself. It is the coefficient before the anomalous current caused by the spin-orbit interaction: \(v_{so} =\frac{\alpha}{\hbar k_F^2}(\bf{\hat{\sigma}} \times \bf{\nabla} V_{imp})\). The gradient in the potential due to impurities results in scattering, or at least that’s how I understand it.

The paper is really a classic kind of theoretical paper: introduce a Hamiltonian, talk a little about what each potential term means, and then do a bunch of calculations. They derive diffusion equations for charge and spin in a metal, and solve them for two “easy” useful cases: a thin strip of metal between two reservoirs, and a thin strip of metal between two tunneling contacts (current incoming from a ferromagnet and going out into a normal metal). For the most part everything is expanded in terms of \(\alpha\), which is posited to be small (if we’re talking about stuff like Al or Cu, it is very much a reasonable approximation).

entry.title: Investigation of nonlocal transport associated with the orbital Hall effect in Ti

link.title: Investigation of nonlocal transport associated with the orbital Hall effect in Ti

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 19

Today’s paper was kind of an unintended read: it is not about the spin Hall effect that I was trying to read up on, but rather orbital Hall effect: charge current can induce a perpendicular flow of orbital angular momentum. The experiment design is comparatively simple: a six terminal titanium Hall bar – a wide central channel and two thin transverse ones, yielding two Hall crosses. Along the first transverse channel they pass a current, across the second they measure voltage. Turns out the measured voltage is significantly higher than would be expected for “Ohmic bypass” – current taking a scenic route in the bar instead of beelining straight through from one terminal to another. And as titanium has a negligibly small SHE, the authors conclude this is evidence for orbital Hall effect: charge current in first transverse wire induces orbital current in the central channel, which by inverse OHE induces a charge current in the second transverse wire.

entry.title: Evidence for non-merger co-evolution of galaxies and their supermassive black holes

link.title: Evidence for non-merger co-evolution of galaxies and their supermassive black holes

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 18

Sometimes I read papers because they are relevant to some problem I’m trying to solve, or a topic I’m interested in. Sometimes I read them because they are referenced a lot in textbooks (for old classic ones), or media (for new trendy ones), and I get curious as to what the original study actually did. Sometimes I read them because I’m bored and browsing the net for giggles (as you may have seen, my sense of humor is very much aligned with the Igs). Today’s paper is a rare case of me choosing a paper to read because of the person who wrote it. I’ve had a bit of a… professional crush? on Dr Becky Smethurst since high school. It’s a rare and very beautiful thing when a person is an awesome science communicator, consistently outputting tons of high quality content, and at the same time an active researcher, actually doing the science they talk about. Very inspiring! Today after watching (still can’t believe my luck that they now have video) the newest episode of The Supermassive Podcast I realised I’ve never actually read any of Dr Becky’s papers, and thought it was time to remedy this omission.

Sooooo, this paper was hard for me *awkward laugh*. Turns out just watching explainers on the topic, even the very best ones, is not enough to fully grasp what’s written in papers, who’d’ve thunk…

What I got was this: there is a well-known correlation between how massive a galaxy’s stars are and how supermassive is the black hole in its centre. And similar correlations exist between SMBH mass and other parameters, like stellar velocities or bulge sizes. But astrophysicists still argue why these correlations appear. The prevailing hypothesis for a time was that the growth of both the black holes and their galaxies was governed by mergers. Something along the lines of “a galaxy merger redistributes angular momentum and feeds both star formation and black hole accretion.” This paper is yet another piece of evidence against the view that the mergers are the only thing that matters. The authors used a (standard?) simulation, which accounts for, frankly, staggering amount of astrophysical phenomena, to get data on ~6800 simulated galaxies. They extracted the ones that had not experienced a merger since redshift 2 (it tickles me how it’s a measure of both distance and time) and the ones that had undergone more than three mergers since then. And then they basically just compared these groups for the correlations between black hole and galaxy evolution. Turned out the galaxies, which have never merged with anyone and kept to themselves their whole life, still had the same-ish correlations with their supermassive black holes as the social butterflies that merged a bunch. Mergers do make the correlations stronger and reduce the scatter, but without them the correlations still persist.

entry.title: Pigeons (Columba livia) as Trainable Observers of Pathology and Radiology Breast Cancer Images

link.title: Pigeons (Columba livia) as Trainable Observers of Pathology and Radiology Breast Cancer Images

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 17

Today’s paper is one of those “could be cool” kinds of experiment. Skinner did get an Ig Nobel for pigeon missiles, after all, so why can’t pigeon histopathologists work just as well? And yup, they do. The experiment design was eerily similar to basic machine learning, complete with dataset augmentation via rotating and flipping the images. Looking at those tissue images myself, I really cannot tell which ones are benign, and which are malignant, but evidently, pigeons, who spent several weeks practicing every day, could do it quite easily. Mammograms proved much harder to distinguish, but human experts kinda struggle with them too. Overall, an impressive performance from the avian “doctors”

entry.title: Fitting A Person Into An NMR Spectrometer

link.title: Fitting A Person Into An NMR Spectrometer

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 16

Today’s paper is from a venerable publication called The Journal of Immaterial Science that since 2021 has been getting out chuckles and snorts immune to the reproducibility crisis. Having worked several years in an NMR lab, I find this particular paper especially hilarious. The fact that the 900 MHz UltraWide-Bore NMR spectrometer actually exists and actually has been used for imaging live rodents is just the icing on the cake XD

entry.title: Magneto-Optical Detection of the Spin Hall Effect in Pt and W Thin Films

link.title: Magneto-Optical Detection of the Spin Hall Effect in Pt and W Thin Films

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 15

Today’s paper is a continuation of my exploration of ways of measuring spin Hall effect. This time, the technique uses magneto-optic Kerr effect: spin Hall effect leads to spin accumulation on the surface of the wire, and thus, if you light the wire up with a laser, the polarization of reflected light rotates. The spatial distribution of accumulated spins depends on sample thickness. So if you measure Kerr rotation for a bunch of samples of various thicknesses, you can extract the spin Hall angle. The coolest part of this technique is that it allows to measure the SHE more or less directly, unlike pretty much every single other method I’ve found so far, which all require the SHE material to interact somehow with a ferromagnet.
